common_name: Crimson Trumpet Vine (Deep Red-Flowered Trumpet Creeper)

planting.note: Plant container stock in spring in well-drained soil in full sun against a large, permanent arbor, wall, or fence; like the species, Crimson Trumpet climbs by aerial rootlets and spreads by root suckers, so give it a dedicated support well away from siding or small trees.

directions: Plant in well-drained, average soil in full sun on a very sturdy, permanent support, since this vigorous woody vine grows quickly into a heavy specimen. Crimson Trumpet is a deeper-flowered selection of the native trumpet creeper, its 3-inch summer blooms opening a richer, more saturated red than the orange-red wild species, which makes it easy to pick out from a distance and especially effective against light-colored walls or fences. It shares the parent species' hummingbird appeal, aerial-rootlet climbing habit, and tendency to spread by root suckers, so site it on masonry or a dedicated large arbor away from wooden structures or small trees. Prune hard in late winter to control size, since flowers form on new growth and hard pruning does not cost the coming season's bloom.

planting.note: Plant container stock in spring in well-drained soil in full sun against a strong, permanent arbor, wall, or fence; Flamenco is a floriferous selection that, like the species, self-clings with aerial rootlets and spreads by root suckers.

directions: Plant in well-drained, average soil in full sun on a strong permanent structure capable of carrying a heavy, long-lived vine. Flamenco bears fiery orange-red, yellow-throated trumpet flowers in dense terminal clusters from midsummer into fall, opening over a longer stretch of the season than many trumpet creeper selections and drawing hummingbirds and butterflies in steady numbers. Left unpruned it can eventually cover a 20-to-30-foot span, so give it a dedicated masonry wall or oversized arbor rather than a house wall or wooden fence, since the clinging aerial rootlets can damage siding over time. Prune back hard in late winter to keep it in bounds; because it flowers on new wood, an annual hard cutback only improves the following season's display.

common_name: Stromboli Trumpet Vine (Compact Dark Red Trumpet Creeper)

planting.note: Plant container stock in spring in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun to light afternoon shade against a sturdy, permanent structure; Stromboli benefits from a sheltered site in the colder half of its range.

directions: Plant in fertile, deep, moist but well-drained soil in full sun, ideally against a warm, sheltered wall in the cooler part of its range. Stromboli produces unusually dense, compact clusters of intensely dark red flowers with short throats marked by fine yellowish veining, a richer and more saturated color than most trumpet creeper cultivars, blooming from midsummer through the first frosts. It is just as vigorous as the wild species, self-clinging by aerial rootlets and capable of covering a large pergola or masonry wall in a few seasons, so match its support and site to its ultimate scale. Prune hard in late winter to control size and shape, since Stromboli blooms on the current year's growth and a severe cutback only encourages a fuller flush of flowers.
sources: North Carolina State Extension — Campsis radicans

planting.note: Plant container-grown vines in spring in fertile, moisture-retentive, well-drained soil in partial shade to full sun against a strong trellis or arbor; this naturally occurring hybrid between A. quinata and A. trifoliata does not come reliably true from seed, so buy vegetatively propagated named stock.

directions: Plant in fertile, moisture-retentive, well-drained soil in partial shade to full sun, giving the twining stems a sturdy trellis, arbor, or pergola to climb since this vigorous hybrid can eventually reach 20 to 30 feet. Akebia x pentaphylla arose as a natural cross between five-leaf and three-leaf akebia and shows intermediate traits of both parents, with leaves bearing three to five leaflets and clusters of fragrant, dark purple, chocolate-and-vanilla-scented flowers opening in mid-spring as the bronze-tinted new foliage emerges. It is semi-evergreen in mild climates and fully deciduous farther north, tolerating shade better than most flowering vines while still flowering well in full sun. Prune back hard after flowering each year to control its vigorous spread and keep it off nearby shrubs, trees, or structures.

planting.note: Plant container vines in late winter or spring in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun to light dappled shade on a sturdy trellis, pergola, or arbor; Clara Mack often blooms in its first year, unusually early for a wisteria.

directions: Plant in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun to light dappled shade on a sturdy support structure; Clara Mack is a white-flowered selection of Wisteria macrostachya, the well-behaved native Kentucky wisteria, found and shared by a South Carolina plantswoman and later introduced into the trade. Its foot-long, lightly fragrant, ivory-white racemes are longer than those of American wisteria (W. frutescens) and open on a plant that is markedly more restrained than Chinese or Japanese wisteria, blooming on new wood so a hard prune never sacrifices the coming season's flowers. Like other Kentucky wisteria selections it twines clockwise, reaches flowering size at a young age, and does not spread invasively into natural areas the way the Asian species do. Give it only annual pruning to shape and control size on a genuinely sturdy long-term support.

planting.note: Plant container vines in late winter or spring in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, moderately fertile soil in full sun on a sturdy trellis, pergola, or arbor; Abbeville Blue is among the most cold-hardy named wisteria selections available.

directions: Plant in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun on a sturdy support structure; Abbeville Blue is a named selection of Wisteria macrostachya prized above all for exceptional winter hardiness, tolerating cold that damages most other wisteria selections and making it a realistic choice for gardeners at the cold edge of wisteria country. Its blue-violet, fragrant racemes tend to open together along the raceme rather than in the more staggered, trailing sequence typical of Japanese wisteria, giving a bold, simultaneous burst of bloom in late spring. Like other Kentucky wisteria selections it twines clockwise and is markedly less aggressive than the invasive Chinese and Japanese species, reaching flowering size at a young age and requiring only annual pruning to control size and shape on a strong, permanent support.

planting.note: Plant container vines in late winter or spring in moderately fertile, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade on a sturdy trellis, pergola, or wall; Kuchibeni (also sold as Lipstick) is a clockwise-twining selection capable of scaling 30 feet given the support to do so.

directions: Plant in moderately fertile, medium-moisture, well-drained soil in full sun or part shade on a very sturdy, permanent support. Kuchibeni, whose Japanese name means 'rouge lips,' bears pale lilac-pink flowers tipped with a deeper violet-purple at the keel, giving each hanging raceme a lipstick-kissed, two-toned look that sets it apart from the more uniformly colored Japanese wisteria cultivars. The pale green spring foliage turns yellow in autumn, and the fragrant racemes can extend to 18 inches on an established vine trained over a large arbor, pergola, or house wall. Prune twice yearly, in summer to control rampant new growth and again in late winter to shape the vine and encourage flower buds, and expect several years before a young plant reaches full flowering maturity.

planting.note: Plant container vines in late winter or spring in moderately fertile, slightly acidic, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade on a sturdy pergola or arbor; Showa-beni is raised from cuttings and typically flowers earlier than seed-grown wisteria.

directions: Plant in moderately fertile, slightly acidic, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade on a sturdy support structure, giving best flowering with as much direct sun as the site allows. Showa-beni is a silky wisteria selection notable for fragrant, lilac-pink flowers marked with a small yellow spot at the center of each bloom, carried on hanging clusters shorter and denser than those of Japanese wisteria, set against soft, velvety, downy-leafleted foliage typical of the species. Because it is propagated from cuttings of a flowering-age plant rather than grown from seed, it reaches bloom sooner than a seedling wisteria of the same age. Prune in summer to control vigorous new growth and again in late winter to shape the vine and encourage next season's flower buds, and provide a genuinely sturdy long-term structure from the start.
